changes: Add the nature of the task and the manager's own preference as factors that shape the choice of style, since the card mentions only urgency and staff experience.
match.reason: The bank card teaches the same three leadership styles and matching them to the situation, but it omits the task and the manager's preference that the new point names, so it needs that addition.

confirm.reason: The bank cards teach NSW's three leadership styles or the contingency approach with different factors, while VCE names five management styles (autocratic, persuasive, consultative, participative, laissez-faire) and four specific factors including the manager's preference, so matching either card would mean changing its content and framing, not just small details.

draft.title: Choosing a management style
card: No single management style is best in every case. A manager chooses a style to suit the situation.
Task and time
a task that is urgent or risky often suits a style where the manager decides alone. A task with time to spare can allow staff to be consulted or to take part in the decision.
Staff experience
skilled, experienced staff can often work well with more say and less supervision. New or unsure staff may need clearer direction from the manager.
Manager's preference
a manager's own beliefs and habits also shape the style they pick. A manager who trusts staff may share decisions more often.
draft.remember: The best style fits the task, the time, the staff and the manager.

a.q: A fire breaks out in a warehouse run by Sam, and staff must leave at once. Why is a style where Sam decides alone most suitable?
opts: The task is urgent, so there is no time to consult staff
The staff are inexperienced, so they need more say
Sam prefers to share decisions with the whole team
Decisions made alone are always better than shared ones
a.why: With an urgent and risky task, there is no time to ask staff for ideas, so deciding alone suits the situation. The last option is tempting, but the card says no style is best in every case, so deciding alone is not always better.
a.clue: Think about how much time Sam has to ask others.

b.q: Priya manages a design studio in Geelong. Her team is highly experienced, and a new project has three months to run. Which approach fits the situation best?
opts: Give the team a large say in how the project is done
Make every decision herself and check each step
Give orders and expect staff to follow without question
Use one style because it suits her, whatever the team
b.why: Experienced staff and plenty of time both suit giving staff more say. Making every decision herself would suit an urgent task or new staff, not this case. Choosing only by her own preference ignores the task, the time and the team.
b.clue: Look at both the staff experience and the time available.

a.best: The task is urgent, so there is no time to consult staff

b.best: Give the team a large say in how the project is done

problems.detail: Why (a) calls the 'always better' option 'the last option', but options are shown in random order. In the order shown, the last option is 'The staff are inexperienced, so they need more say'. The why should name the option by its wording, not its position.
The distractor 'Decisions made alone are always better than shared ones' uses 'always' where the card says 'often'. The why does refute it, so this is minor, but it is listed as required.
